full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: We heard the above appeals together, one after another, and now dispose of them by this judgment.

FA No. 303 of 2000

2. Third Defendant, the Korea Exchange Bank (KEB), Seoul, Korea, presented the appeal against the decree dated 2-11-99 passed by Subordinate Judge and First Commercial Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 10 of 1993, which decreed the suit.

3. On 12-9-93 the plaintiff Gemini Garments Ltd, in brief, Gemini, instituted the suit against the appellant and others for a decree of declaration that first defendant, Pubali Bank Ltd (PBL) shall not pay the moneys due under the letter of credit No. PBL/LO/ST/114/93 dated 9-5-93 to said third defendant, KEB and also for a decree of perpetual injunction for restraining PBL from paying any money under said letter of credit to third defendant.

4. Plaint case, in short, is that Gemini opened said irrevocable LC for US $ 194,337.29 C&F at Chittagong for import of fabrics and accessories favouring second defendant, Daily Enterprise Co. Ltd, Seoul, South Korea (seller) through the issuing bank, PBL which transmitted the letter of credit via their correspondent, the Chemical Bank, Seoul, South Korea to third defendant KEB. The letter of credit was established on the back of a master letter of credit No. 6005696745K2 opened by Dr Rehfeld Handelsgaselschaft MBH. Hamburg through Deutschbank, Hamburg which was partly transferred to the plaintiff Gemini for US $ 228.824.70 by the prime beneficiary, YK Garments Ltd of Dhaka.

5. Issuing bank PBL received the drafts drawn by the seller along with shipping documents in 5 separate lots from the KEB. Gemini received the documents despite certain discrepancies, namely, (a) Forwarders Bills of Lading sent instead of Clean shipped on Board Ocean Bill of Lading, (b) shipment made after expiry of the shipment date, and (c) two instead of four packing lists in respect of one lot, namely, FBL No. BUCH-1049. On 27-6-93 PBL communicated its acceptance dated 26-6-93 by registered airmail giving due date for payment on 28-9-93; 1-10-93; 8-10-93; 22-9-93 and 15-10-93 respectively.

6. Further case of the plaintiff is that second defendant seller was also acting as agent of Gemini in Dhaka. Accordingly, the seller set up an office at Dhaka. One Mr IJ Choi was working as manager at Dhaka office of the seller. On 29-6-93 one Mr DW Kim visited the office of Gemini and held discussion about the production planning of the orders. As the discussion could not be finished, he promised to come back on 3-7-93. When he did not turn up. managing director enquired of him and learnt that all the Korean staffs of the office secretly left Dhaka.

7. Smelling foul play, Gemini advised PBL to convey its non-acceptance of the documents by telex to supersede its earlier acceptance and on 3-7-93 PBL transmitted non-acceptance by telex. Gemini believed that in all likelihood the cancellation reached the negotiating bank earlier to the acceptance.

8. Gemini further claimed that it discovered that the documents forwarded by the KEB were fraudulent inasmuch as "freight pre-paid" was falsely entered in all five bills of lading without any freight paid and "on board" marked in two bills of lading, namely, FBL BUCH-1064 and FBL-1065 without any goods put on board i.e. shipped. The KEB thereby intentionally avoided mentioning that it has accepted the fake documents of shipment.

9. Further, fourth defendant Yulim Shipping Co Ltd through its agent in Bangladesh informed Gemini that the seller became bankrupt by the time and all the staffs of the seller left without settling the freight of the cargoes.

First defendant, PBL and third defendant, KEB contested the suit by filing two separate written statements.

10. PBL contended that it received five sets of shipping documents covering the letter of credit. PBL obtained acceptance of the plaintiff Gemini in all aforesaid five sets of shipping documents and sent its acceptance by its registered airmail letter dated 26-6-93 posted on 27-6-93. Gemini then by its letter dated 3-7-93 notified PBL of certain discrepancies in the shipping documents and advised PBL to send a telex to third defendant KEB communicating non-acceptance of the documents. On the same date PBL sent a telex to third defendant KEB communicating its non-acceptance of all five sets of shipping documents thereby superseding its earlier acceptance sent by registered airmail. The PBL informed KEB that the letter dated 26-6-93 ought to be treated as cancelled as the applicant of the letter of credit declined to accept the documents due to reasons that (a) forwarder bill of lading was submitted instead of 'clean shipped on board ocean bill of lading' and (b) shipment made after the expiry of the shipment date. PBL accordingly, advised third defendant KEB that its earlier acceptance should be treated as withdrawn and/or null and void. It also hoped that the acceptance posted on 27-6-93 was unlikely to reach third defendant KEB before receipt of the telex dated 3-7-93 and said acceptance was the result of bona fide and inadvertent oversight of manifest discrepancies which were pointed out to third defendant KEB. Besides, said acceptance was induced by fraudulent and forged documents.

11. Further, it contended that on arrival of two consignments of the goods, the carrier refused to deliver the goods on the ground that the freight was outstanding whereas the letter of credit provided for the bill of lading should be freight pre-paid and clean shipped on board. Upon enquiry, it revealed that out of five consignments, two consignments covering US $ 57,025.79 actually reached at Chittagong and one consignment covering US $ 17,990.40 was reported to be 'on transit' in Singapore, which did not in fact reach Chittagong. Remaining two consignments namely FBL BUCH-1064 and BUCH-I065 were never shipped at all. Those consignments covered major portion of the letter of credit being for US $ 1,19,321.10. Third defendant KEB negotiated the documents, which were manifestly discrepant in violation of the terms and conditions of the letter of credit. Moreover, purported negotiations were done by 17-6-93 long before their acceptance dated 26-6-93.

12. Denying the plaint case, third defendant KEB contended that the freight forwarder bill of lading was as good as was clean bill of lading. It denied that two instead of four copies of packing list were provided.

13. It further contended that upon receipt of the papers and documents, Gemini or first defendant PBL failed to refuse the documents within reasonable time, as such, they were deemed to have accepted the documents. Five bills of lading which were issued by fourth defendant Yulim Shipping Company were all Fiata Combined Transport Bill of Lading approved by the International Chamber of Commerce and, as such, they were as good as on board ocean bill of lading under the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit.

14. The arrival of second defendant's staff Mr DW Kim at the office of Gemini on 29-6-03 and his subsequent failure to turn up on 3-7-93 were beyond the knowledge of KEB. It claimed that registered letter dated 27-6-93 reached the KEB on Friday that is on 2-7-93. The telex dated 3-7-93 reached the KEB at 5-54 PM on the same day which was Saturday and was received by KEB at 9-00 AM on Monday that is 5-7-93 because of the fact that the banks in Korea remained closed from 1-30 PM on Saturday until 9-00 AM of Monday. The branch office of KEB that handled the matter received the telex on Tuesday, that is 6-7-93. First defendant on behalf of seller refused five sets of documents respectively after 35 days, 29 days, 29 days, 21 days and 13 days of receipt of the documents by them. In any event, first defendant PBL accepted the documents long before the letter dated 26-6-93 was posted.

On the pleadings following issues were settled:

(a) was the suit maintainable in the manner and form as framed?

(b) was the suit barred by limitation?

(c) was any fraud committed in respect of letter of credit in question?

(d) was the plaintiff entitled to relief prayed for?

(e) what relief the plaintiff was entitled to?

15. Plaintiff Gemini and first defendant PBL examined one witness each while the KEB examined four witnesses in support of their respective cases.

16. Papers and documents adduced by the plaintiff were marked Exhibit 1 to 12 while those of the defendants marked Exhibit A to F series, and X.

17. PW 1, Fazle Hossain testified in support of the plaint case. He said that PBL received five lots of shipping documents from third defendant KEB on different dates, namely, on 25-5-93, 31-5-93, 2-6-93, 10-6-93 and 16-6-93. The documents included five bills of lading. Excepting the first one dated 25-5-93, all shipments were effected after expiry of last date of shipment. They wanted clean shipped on board bills of lading but the seller sent forwarders bills of lading. All the bills of lading required by the letter of credit to be marked and were so marked 'freight pre-paid'. But no freight was paid.

18. He deposed that second defendant seller was also acting as agent of Gemini. Accordingly, they rented a house at House No. 49, Road No. 1A, Banani, Dhaka. Mr IJ Choi was the manager and he visited their factory for the purpose of opening back to back letter of credit. On 23-6-93 another staff DW Kim came to their office to discuss the production planning but the discussion could not be completed on that day and he said he would come back on 3-7-93 but he did not turn up. He then telephoned their local office at Banani and he was told by local staff that all the Korean people had secretly left. He then contacted first defendant PBL to enquire of the matter. PBL informed him that they had given acceptance of the documents on 26- 6-93 posted on 27-6-93. He then advised PBL to send a telex to third defendant KEB revoking the acceptance on the ground of discrepancies. Third defendant KEB replied on 10-7-93. PBL sent them a telex of that reply by their letter dated 11-7-93.

19. They accepted the documents keeping in mind that he had to deliver goods to a German buyer by the end of July, 1993. They found the bills of lading were stamped freight pre-paid and shipped on board. They sent all documents to their CRF agent. Their agent came back and told him that local agent of the Shippers Bengal Shipping Line declined to issue delivery order for the goods from the port on the ground of non-payment of freight. All the bills of lading showed freight pre-paid but the shipper agent said, in fact, the freight was not paid in respect of all five consignments. Two consignments out of the five consignments were never shipped on board whereas the relevant bills of lading were clearly marked shipped on board.

20. Fourth defendant shipper's agent sent them a fax on 20-7-93, Exhibit 5. Third defendant KEB negotiated discrepant documents and in this regard first defendant PBL sent numerous telex messages to third defendant KEB declining payment for the fraudulent documents submitted. The letter of revocation sent by the telex on 3-7-93 reached the KEB before letter of acceptance dated 26-6-93. The letter dated 21-7-93 of fourth defendant read no freight was paid and two consignments under said bills of lading were never shipped, Exhibit 6. Third defendant KEB by telex message dated 15-7-93 informed the PBL that they were trying their best to enable the plaintiff Gemini to receive the delivery orders for the cargo. On 27-8-93 fourth defendant the shipping line wrote Gemini to cancel the letter of credit in respect of two bills of lading being Nos. 1064 and 1065, Exhibit 10. First defendant PBL refused payment on 7-9-93, Exhibit 11.

21. He further claimed that third defendant colluded with second and fourth defendants to have the documents accepted. All five shipments under five bills of lading constituted one consignment under one letter of credit. Unless all the five shipments reached Gemini, the contract under the letter of credit was not fulfilled. It was useless for the plaintiff to receive any part delivery.

22. In cross-examination, he testified that he was working as managing director of Gemini for more than ten years. He was more or less acquainted with letter of credit matter. In the body of the letter of credit, third defendant KEB was not mentioned but the documents were negotiated by said KEB. Third defendant KEB was the banker of the seller. They knew from the very beginning that the documents were discrepant. They accepted the documents on 24/25-6-93. On 3-7-93 they discovered the fraud. He did not mention to first defendant PBL that the documents were forged because they were examining whether or not there was actually any fraud. Gemini informed first defendant about the fraud few days after 3-7-93. On 12-7-93 he discovered fraud. On the same day he informed his banker. It was not a fact that they discovered fraud on 28 July, 1993.

23. It was his case that defendant No. 2 became bankrupt. He came to know about it through fax, which was sent by fourth defendant, shipper Bengal Shipping Line. Fourth defendant was his only source of knowledge about bankruptcy of the seller. He did not make any independent attempt to find out the bankruptcy of the seller. Fourth defendant was the shipping agent of second defendant seller. Second defendant seller did not pay the sea freight. The fact that they came to know from the letter of fourth defendant, Exhibit 5 and also from the letter of the Bengal Shipping Lines dated 21-7-93.

24. DW 1 Md Abul Kalam testified on behalf of the issuing bank, PBL. Besides deposing in support of the written statement, he testified that the PBL received five sets of documents. First set of documents valued at US $ 30,695.00; second set of documents valued at US $ 17,990.00; third set of documents valued at US $ 36,263.30; fourth set of documents valued at US $ 28,284.00 and fifth set of documents valued at 91,037.00. Upon receipt of the documents, PBL sent its acceptance to the negotiating bank. The letter of acceptance was dated 26-6-93, which was dispatched on 27-6-93 by airmail. They received a letter from Gemini regarding non-acceptance of the documents due to some major discrepancies. Immediately after receipt of the letter, they sent a telex message on 3-7-93 requesting non-acceptance and to treat the acceptance as null and void, Exhibit 3(b). Subsequently, by several telexes dated 13-7-93, 15-7-93, 25-7-93, 24-7-93 and 5-8-93 they reiterated their non-acceptance. After 3-7-93, the next working day in Korea was 5-7-93. Since the postal article was dropped in the GPO Box of third defendant and it subsequently reached respective branch of third defendant KEB on 5-7-93. Out of five sets, balance two sets of document amounting to 70% of letter of credit value. Fourth defendant issued the bills of lading without receiving any freight. The cargo was not ready for shipment. Third defendant KEB negotiated discrepant documents even before. their acceptance in violation of the instructions mentioned in the letter of credit. Last two consignments were not shipped. Third defendant presented fraudulent documents to PBL without searching the goods on board. He denied that third defendant had no knowledge about the fraud at any stage.

25. In cross-examination; he stated that he did not make any payment because documents were fraudulent and discrepant. They cancelled the acceptance immediately after they learnt of the fraud. The KEB negotiated the documents on 25-5-93 for US $ 30,695; on 31-5-93 for US $ 13,200; on 3-6-93 for US $ 26,632; on 10-6-93 for US $ 28,284 and on 17-6-93 for US $ 91,037. On 13-9-93 they received a notice of injunction not to effect any payment.

26. Clause J was incorporated in the letter of credit outside all the common banking practices. Upon receipt of the documents they informed the Gemini to retire the documents. They rejected the documents on the basis of documents alone on 3-7-93. They rejected the first lot of the documents after 34 days of receipt thereof, second lot after 27 days, third lot after 27 days, fourth lot after 20 days and fifth lot after 11 days.

27. DW 2 Mahmudul lslam brought the record of delivery of the registered letters. Unregistered letter, Exhibit C was delivered to the recipient on 3-7-93. He had no personal knowledge of the statement.

28. DW 3 Md Rokanuddin, Superintendent, Investigation, Section I, Post Master General Office, Central Circle, Dhaka. He proved his signature on Exhibit C.

29.	DW 4 Delwar Hossain proved Exhibit C.

30.	DW 5 Mirza Kamrul Hasan who deposed on behalf of third defendant KEB. He testified on the basis of power of attorney given by KEB. He had no direct knowledge about the case. He deposed on the basis of papers submitted by third defendant KEB and instructions given to him. According to his knowledge, documents to reach from Korea to Dhaka should not take 48 hours. He also produced the documents on behalf of third defendant KEB. Third defendant KEB did not receive any communication from first defendant PBL refusing the documents within seven days. Third defendant KEB received the letter of acceptance dated 26-6-93 on 2-7-93 but they had no evidence to show to the Court that on 2-7-93 they received the letter. The telex was dated 3-7-93 at 5-54 PM Bangladesh time. Office of third defendant KEB remained closed when the telex was transmitted. Their office remained closed from 1-30 PM on Saturday until Monday at 9-00 AM. Head office received it on 5-7-93.

31.	He also said that they had no knowledge about the bankruptcy of second defendant seller. He had no knowledge whether the goods were shipped or not because, the bank dealt with documents not with the goods. They accepted forwarder bills of lading instead of clean ship on board and ocean bills of lading because both were the same. They accepted four copies of packing list instead of two. He denied that third defendant KEB negotiated discrepant documents. KEB negotiated the documents under reserve under clause J of the letter of credit because it was a claim that applied between third defendant KEB and the seller. The documents negotiated by KEB were not fraudulent. It was not correct to say the acceptance of LC documents was induced by fraud.

32.	In cross-examination, he denied that they had not paid under the letter of credit. He did not know when they paid. It was not true that third defendant KEB had not made any payment to the seller. He had no document to show actual payment was made or money was transferred by KEB to the seller vide Exhibit F series.

33. On the aforesaid pleadings and the evidence oral and documentary on record, learned Subordinate Judge found that third defendant KEB negotiated the documents before receipt of the acceptance by first defendant PBL in violation of the terms of the letter of credit from 25th May to 17th June, 1993; that the documents submitted were discrepant and fraudulent; and that first defendant PBL was not obliged to pay on the discrepant and fraudulent documents.

34. Upon such view, the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit declaring that first defendant PBL shall not pay any money under the letter of credit to third defendant KEB and permanently restrained first defendant PBL from making any payment under the letter of credit to third defendant KEB. Hence, the appeal.

FA No. 352 of 2001

Aforesaid third defendant KEB also presented this appeal against the decree dated 30-1-2001 passed by Subordinate Judge and First Commercial Court in Title Suit No.9 of 1993, which decreed the suit.

36. On 12-9-93 respondent No. 1 Southern Apparels Ltd as plaintiff, in brief, Southern, instituted Title Suit No. 9 of 1993, for a similar decree of declaration that first defendant Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd (ABBL) shall not pay the moneys under two letters of credit Nos. 183/93 and 199/93 dated 12-5-93 and 22-5-93 to third defendant KEB and also for a perpetual injunction restraining said ABBL from paying any money under said letters of credit.

37. Plaint case, in short, was that Southern received two master letters of credit being 600/569645K2 and 33-95076 dated 13-4-1993 and 8-4-1993 amounting US $ 397,481.60 and US $ 51,194.40 respectively. The letters of credit were transferred by the prime beneficiary YK Garments Ltd of Dhaka. First one was opened by Dr Rehfeld Handelgasselschaft MBH, Modem 5 Hamburg 61 through Deutschbank, Hamburg while the latter by M Oelhafen AG, Birsfelden, Switzerland.

38. Against said master letters of credit, Southern established aforesaid two back to back letters of credit being Nos. MJ/EXP/BB/183/93 and MJ/EXP/BB/199/93 dated 12-5-1993 and 22-5-1993 respectively through the ABBL in favour of second defendant Daily Enterprise Co Ltd, Seoul, Korea (seller) for import of fabrics and accessories for a total amount of US $ 300,913.14.

39. The seller sent six sets of documents through the negotiating bank, third defendant KEB for payment of US $ 2,22,477.72. All the bills of lading clearly marked that goods were shipped "On Board" and "Freight Pre-paid". Southern sent those documents to its clearing agent in Chittagong for clearance of the goods. But the clearing agent could not release the goods as the ocean freight remained unpaid by the seller and the consignments under bills of lading No. BUCH 1063 and BUCH 1066 could not be traced as the goods were not shipped. Southern, therefore, claimed that the acceptance of the documents was induced by fraud. Southern consequently, suffered a loss of US $ 170,000. Southern then returned the documents to ABBL requesting to cancel the acceptance communicated earlier. The ABBL however on 13-7-1993 wrote to them that they could not accept the request. The ABBL by letter dated 3-8-1993 informed the plaintiff that the KEB already negotiated the documents and they claimed payments on the maturity dates. The consignments under four bilIs of lading which arrived could not be released as freight was not paid though the bilIs of lading were clearly marked that "Freight Pre-paid". The KEB having negotiated the discrepant documents was not entitled to payment.

40. Denying the plaint case first defendant ABBL and third defendant KEB filed two separate written statements.

41. First defendant ABBL contended that Southern opened two letters of credit dated 12-5-1993 and 22-5-1993 for value at US $ 266,687.12 and US $ 34,226.02 respectively through them in favour of second defendant seller in total amounting to US $ 300,913.14. ABBL received six sets of documents inclusive of forwarder bills of lading issued by fourth defendant through the negotiating bank KEB for acceptance and payment of US $ 2,22,477.77. All the forwarder bills of lading were clearly marked accepted 'on board' and 'freight pre-paid'. They received the documents and communicated their acceptance dated from 7-6-1993 to 26-6-1993 and date of maturity from 22-9-1993 to 14-10-1993.

42. It further contended that the consignments under FBL BUCH 1063 and 1066 were never shipped from Bushan although concerned FBLs were marked 'on board'. Four consignments out of six arrived at Chittagong and remaining two would never come.

43. Third defendant KEB contended that they had no knowledge about freight of the consignments remained unpaid by the seller and non-arrival of two consignments under the bills of lading being BUCH 1063 and BUCH 1066. It also contended that they already negotiated the documents and they sent copies of outward bills register with the shipping documents and drafts to the first defendant ABBL by DHL Courier Service with the following clear instruction either to accept or reject the document.

* Cable us in case of non-payment/non-acceptance giving reasons

* Advise us by cable/airmail of acceptance and due date in case of usance bill.

44. It contended that upon receiving the documents first defendant ABBL at its free will and express knowledge and consent of Southern accepted them and communicated its acceptance to third defendant KEB by telex message dated 7th June, 24th June and 26th June, 1993 together with the maturity dates i.e. dates on which first defendant undertook unconditionally to pay third defendant KEB.

45. It also contended that first defendant ABBL had reasonable time to examine the documents and take decision either to accept or reject the documents. The allegations of fraud was made for the first time on 21-7-1993 after a period of 54 days, 47 days, 45 days, 38 days and 31 days respectively of the receipt of the documents and 44 days, 27 days and 25 days respectively communicating the acceptance by three telex messages to third defendant KEB.

46. On the pleadings following issues were settled:

(a) was the suit maintainable in the present form and manner as framed?

(b) was the suit barred by limitation?

(c) was any fraud committed by the defendants?

and

(d) was the plaintiff entitled to get any relief as prayer for?

47. Plaintiff Southern, first defendant ABBL and third defendant KEB examined one witness each. Documents adduced by Southern were marked Exhibit 1 to 10 series while those of defendants Exhibit A to D series.

48. On behalf of Southern, PW 1 Abdus Sakur was examined. He testified in support of the plaint case. He stated that they received two master letters of credit from the buyer, Exhibit 3 series. Against these master letters of credit they opened two back to back letters of credit through first defendant ABBL for import of raw materials and accessories, Exhibit 4 series. They received six sets of shipping documents, Exhibit 5 series. Forwarder bills of lading clearly marked 'on board' and 'freight pre-paid'. Those were sent by third defendant KEB, the negotiating bank. Fourth defendant, Yulim Shipping Company acted as agent of second defendant seller. Out of six consignments, four arrived at Chittagong and two consignments were untraceable. Consignments could not be cleared since freight was not paid although the FBLs clearly marked 'freight pre-paid' and 'on board'. By letters and faxes dated 19-7-1993, 17-7-1993 and 18-7-1993 Bengal Shipping Limited, an agent of fourth defendant Yulim Shipping Company, confirmed the fraud, Exhibit 6 series. Fourth defendant Yulim Shipping Company Limited by a letter dated 19-7-1993 informed them that second defendant seller became bankrupt. ABBL returned all shipping documents by a letter dated 3-8-1993 saying that KEB negotiated the documents and they claimed payment on maturity dates, Exhibit 7.

49. In cross-examination, he stated that he accepted the documents on 7-6-1993. Their bank communicated the acceptance through telex dated 7-9-1993 with regard to consignment FBL 1050. They did not pay any payment to ABBL after receiving those documents. ABBL did not ask for any payment. They filed the documents in the Court that second defendant seller became bankrupt.

50. DW 1 Mirza Kamrul Hasan deposed on behalf of third defendant KEB as attorney on the basis of a power of attorney. He stated that they sent the documents to ABBL by outward registered schedules dated 25-5-1993, 31-5-1993, 3-6-1993, 10-6-1993, 12-6-1993 and 17-6-1993 through DHL courier service. The ABBL accepted the documents and gave them maturity dates of payment of all six bills of lading by telex dated 7-6-1993, 24-6-1993 and 26-6-1993, Exhibit C series. There was no discrepancy in their documents. He did not have any knowledge of fraud at all. They had no knowledge that the bills of lading were obtained without placing the goods on board. They had no knowledge whether consignments under FBL BUCH 1063 and BUCH 1066 were not shipped from Bushan, Korea. He had no knowledge of letters dated 18-7-1993 and 19-7-1993 written by various parties to Southern. He had no knowledge about consignments of the goods, which did not arrive in Bangladesh. He produced six instruments of transfer of money from third defendant KEB to second defendant seller in . Korean language with English version, Exhibit D series.

51. In cross-examination, he stated that in Exhibit D period was shown 92 days dated 25-5-1993, Exhibit D1 92 days dated 3-6-1993, Exhibit D2 92 days dated 31-5-1993, Exhibit D3 92 days dated 12-6-1993, Exhibit D4 92 days dated 10-6-1993 and Exhibit D5 92 days dated 17-6-1993. Under the LC Exhibit 4 payment was to be made 120 days after sight. So the payment was not made in terms of the letter of credit. He denied that they acted against the instructions of the letters of credit. They filed no papers to show that second defendant seller received money other than Exhibit D series. It showed that money was transferred to the account of the seller.

52. DW 2 ASM Mahbubur Rahman deposed on behalf of first defendant ABBL. He deposed that as per terms of the letter of credit they received six sets of documents from third defendant KEB and in time handed over to Southern. Southern did not raise any objection at the time of receipt of the documents. But subsequently, by a letter dated 18-7-1993 Southern informed that consignments against four sets of documents goods arrived but against other two sets did not arrive. They informed third defendant KEB of the dates of maturity as per terms of the letters of credit. They also informed the objection of Southern to third defendant KEB. After return of the documents, third defendant KEB demanded payment from them.

53. In cross-examination, he stated that there were no discrepancies in the documents, according to them. Southern received documents by putting its signature. Then, they communicated the acceptance to third defendant KEB giving the maturity dates.

54. On the aforesaid pleadings and evidence, oral and documentary, on record, learned Subordinate Judge held that third defendant KEB could not prove that any payment was made to second defendant seller; that fraud was committed by the defendants; that second defendant seller became bankrupt and that the plaintiff Southern was entitled to the declaration sought for and perpetual injunction.

55. Upon such findings, the learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit as prayed for declaring first defendant ABBL shall not pay money due under said two letters of credit Nos. 183/93 and 199/93 dated 12-5-1993 and 22-5-1993 to third defendant KEB and first defendant ABBL was also permanently restrained from making any payment of money under said letters of credit to third defendant KEB.

Submissions

56. In both FA No. 303 of 2000 and FA No. 352 of 2001 though first respondent applicants, namely, Gemini and Southern, and the issuing banks, namely, PBL and ABBL, are different but the beneficiary, Daily Enterprise Co, seller and the appellant KEB are the same and the issues raised are also the same.

57. On behalf of said appellant, Mr Abdur A Rezzaque, learned Senior Advocate, submitted that in view of Order VI rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, no fraud having been pleaded in the plaint nor claimed against the appellant of being in anyway concerned with any fraud and in FA No. 303 of 2000 the documents having never been rejected on ground of fraud, the learned Joint District Judge erred in law in decreeing the suit on fraud. In support, he cited AIR 1941 PC 93.

58. He submitted that payment under a letter of credit could only be refused on the ground of established and real fraud before acceptance of the documents and not otherwise under DCP 400.

59. He submitted that in FA No. 303 of 2000 the issuing bank PBL first communicated its acceptance after considerable time of receipt of the documents by its letter dated 26-6-1993, which reached the KEB before its telex dated 3-7-1993 cancelling the acceptance not even on ground of fraud rather on ground of some discrepancies and such late cancellation would be of no avail to protect the PBL from honouring its obligation under the letter of credit.

60. He submitted that under UCP 400 the KEB having admittedly negotiated the documents even before receiving the acceptance by the PBL could not be denied payment, particularly in view of clauses (C) and (D) of the letter of credit.

61. As the letter of credit required for negotiating the documents within fifteen days of shipment and the KEB having negotiated on the same date of receipt and dispatch of the documents under reserve and the PBL having not rejected the documents within reasonable time rather accepted them, the PBL would be precluded from raising any objection under clause (f) of article 16 of UCP 400, he submitted.

62. He submitted that had the PBL rejected the documents within reasonable time, then the KEB could be said to have to be reimbursed by the beneficiary seller under clause (f) of article 16 of UCP 400.

63. 92. On the learned deliberations of senior members of the Bar, we shall have to first find the law to determine the rights and obligations of the parties involved in the transactions.

93. In all the cases, the letters of credit were made subject to Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, 1983 revision, and ICC Publication No. 400, in short, UCP 400.

<u>94. The letter of credit has developed over the experience of centuries in the international trade and commerce. It operates to secure the payment to the seller for the price of the goods sold. It also protects the corresponding interest of the buyer and the paying bank. The bank issuing the credit undertakes to honour and pay when the demand is made by the seller as per terms and conditions of the letter of credit. Payment by letter of credit has become so effective and secured mode of payment in international trade that in RD Harbottle (Mercantile) Ltd and another vs National West minster Bank Ltd and others, [J977] 2 All ER 862 Justice Kerr termed the instrument as "the blood of international commerce." With due respect, the instrument of letter of credit appears to us as the lifeline in international trade and commerce.</u>

95. In order to fully comprehend the implications of the principles, we must first read certain articles of UCP 400.

96. Article 1 of UCP 400 provides, inter alia, if the UCP 400 is incorporated in a documentary credit, then result would be that all its articles will stand applicable in such credit and binding on all parties thereto unless otherwise expressly agreed.

97. Under article 2 of said UCP 400, all sorts of documentary credits or standby letter(s) of credit shall mean any arrangement, whereby the issuing bank at the request and on the instructions of a customer (the applicant)

I.	is to make a payment to or to the order of a third party, (the beneficiary), or is to pay or accept bills of exchange (drafts) drawn by the beneficiary,

lI. 	authorises another bank to effect such payment, or to pay, accept or negotiate such bills of exchange (drafts),

against stipulated I®cum..ents, provided that the terms and conditions of the credit are complied with.

Article 3 reads,

"Credits, by their nature, are separate transactions from the sales or other contract(s) on which they may be based and banks are in no way concerned with or bound by such contract(s), even if reference whatsoever to such contract(s) is included in the credit."

Article 4 reads,

"In credit operations all parties concerned deal in documents, and not in goods service and/or other performance to which the documents may relate."

98. The independence of the credit is secured in its operation under article 3 by expressly providing that by nature the contract brought into existence by opening a letter of credit is completely separate from the contract of sale or service though the former is based on and necessitated for the latter, for obvious reasons. Secondly, the banks are no way concerned with or made bound by such contract of sale or service. Thirdly, under article 4, in the operation of the credit, all parties concerned or having privy to such newer contract deal in documents and not in goods, service and/or performance the documents may relate to.

<u>99. If articles 3 and 4 are read together, the intention becomes very clear that the letter of credit issued must be independent or autonomous of the underlying contract of sale of goods or service and the banks concerned with such credit are to deal in documents and not in goods.</u>

100.	Sanctity and security of the letter of credit are founded on two cardinal principles, namely, (a) the independence of the credit and (b) the doctrine of strict compliance.

101.	Article 15 reads,

"Banks must examine all documents with reasonable care to ascertain that they appear on their face to be in accordance with the terms and conditions of the credit. Documents which appear on their face to be inconsistent with one another will be considered as not appearing on their face to be in accordance with the terms and conditions of the credit."

102. The article requires of the issuing bank to examine all documents produced for payment with reasonable care to determine that the documents on their face appear to be in accordance with the terms and conditions of the credit and the documents which appear on their face inconsistent with one another will be considered as not appearing on their face to be in accordance with the terms and conditions of the credit. When the documents produced strictly comply with the terms and conditions of the credit, only then the issuing or paying bank is obliged to pay in terms of the credit. Such bank is therefore always entitled to refuse payment when the documents produced for payment do not strictly conform to the terms and conditions of the credit, wherefrom the doctrine of strict compliance evolved. This makes it certain, the paying bank will not pay the seller unless the seller presents documents which strictly conform strictly to the requirements in the letter of credit. The bank is also protected because it is not required to make any judgment on as substantial compliance.

103. For example, it was held in Equitable Trust Company of New York vs Dawson Partners Ltd, [1927] 2 Lloyd's Law Report 49 at 52 Lord Sumner encapsulates the doctrine "that there is no room for documents which are almost the same or which will do just as well". In Sopoma Spa vs Marine and Animal By-products Corporation, [1966] J Lloyd's Law Report 367 the Court of Appeal found the bank right to refuse the payment as the bill of lading marked 'freight collect' instead of 'freight prepaid'. Similarly, in Commercial Banking Company of Sydney Ltd vs Jalsard Pvt Ltd, [1973] AC 279 Lord Diplock rules, "the banker is not concerned whether the documents for which the buyer has stipulated serve any useful commercial purpose or as to why the customer called for the tender of a document of a particular description. Both the issuing banker and his correspondent bank have to make quick decisions as to whether a document which has been tendered by the seller complies with the requirements of a credit."

104. When the performance of the beneficiary is not in strict compliance with the letter of credit, the paying bank is obliged to the applicant to reject the documents and refuse the payment on the letter of credit.

105. Result being, when the seller presents documents complying with the requirements in the letter of credit, the seller will receive the payment from the paying bank irrespective of any developments in the underlying contract of sale or the relationship between the seller or buyer. The relationship between the seller and issuing bank on the basis of the letter of credit is completely independent of all relationships between the seller, buyer and issuing bank.

106. A letter of credit involves at least three separate and independent transactions giving rise to three relationships among three set of parties:

1.	the contract between the buyer and the seller, which necessitates the issuing of the letter of credit,

2.	the contract between buyer and the issuing bank for issuing a letter of credit to the seller and

3.	the contract between the issuing bank and the seller by which such bank undertakes to pay the seller.

107. There may be other transactions or relationships to develop around the letter of credit but all of them would revolve round these contracts. For breach, each of the contracts is enforceable independent of other two contracts against the parties or privies thereto only.

108. Keeping in mind the sanctity and independence of the letter of credit, the Court never interferes with the normal operation and/or working of the letter of credit. Any dispute between the seller and buyer must be left for them to settle. The banks cannot be dragged into such disputes. But experience forced the Court to carve out an exception to the rule of independence, which is popularly known as fraud exception. In case the seller is found to be unscrupulous and/or guilty of fraud in dealing with the buyer, it would be unconscionable to insist that the bank should make payment. In Sztejn vs Henry Schroder Banking Corporation, 31 NYS 2nd 631 (1941) Mr Shientag J ruled that the principle of independence of the bank's obligation under the letter of credit should not be extended to protect the unscrupulous seller.' The principle is largely based upon the old maxims, 'ex turpi causa non oritur actio' i.e. a person cannot found an action on his own fraudulent behaviour and 'fraus omina corrumpit' meaning fraud unravels all.

109. The essence of the exception is that the bank can either avoid or be prevented from making payment. The exception is available both as defence by the bank to avoid a demand for payment or as injunction or interdict by a party to prevent the bank from making payment. Essential requirement is that the beneficiary's fraudulent conduct is dearly established (Edward Owen Engineering Ltd "S Barc/ays Bank International Ltd, [1978] 1 Lloyd's Rep 166 at 170-1 72=[1978] 1 All ER 976). Mere allegation of fraud is however not sufficient. Fraud must be apparent (United Trading Corporation SA and Murray Clayton Ltd vs Allied Arab Banks, [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 554 at 560). And the bank must have notice of the fraud before making payment on the credit.

110. In spite of recognition of the fraud exception in the transactions based on documentary edits, debates continued as to the ambits and applications of the exception. There may be fraud in respect of documents and in the underlying transaction. In America, old articles 5-114 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) prior to revision failed to define the concept of fraud in transaction. The recently revised Articles 5-109 specifically provides that a bank can dishonour a letter of credit if payment would facilitate a material fraud by the beneficiary on the issuing or paying bank or the applicant. In other words, fraud need not be contained in the documents presented. This ended a long standing debate as to whether fraud in the underlying transaction could warrant non-payment by a bank. Now, it is recognised in all jurisdictions that fraud may exist in respect of presentation of documents as well as in the contract of sale that underlay the letter of credit. Payment may be refused and/or injuncted not only in case of forged or fraudulent documents, but also in case of any material fraud by the beneficiary on the issuing bank or the buyer (applicant).

111. The UCP governs the international transactions based on documentary credit but is silent in respect of the fraud exception. Reason may be, it compiled the customs and practice in dealing with such credit, which developed over the centuries. It is not a codification of rules as such. There is no reason to think that the bank leaders are not aware of the magnitude of fraud in international trade and commerce. But it is not their domain to legislate against fraud. Fraud is of universal connotation having the same meaning on every land. But question of fraud could only be decided by law of the lands.

112.In America:

In America, the fraud exception was recognised through case-law and then, codified in the Uniform Commercial Code, in brief, UCC. In England, the exception is mainly based upon the common law principle that no one should benefit from his own fraud or fraudulent conduct.

113. Fraud exception first found its recognition and application in the seminal case of Sztejn vs J Henry Schroder Banking Corporation et; 177 Miscellaneous 71 9, NYS 2d 631 or [1941] 31 NYS 2nd 631 before the Supreme Court of New York County, New York. The applicant for a credit claimed an injunction against the issuing bank to prevent it paying on the documents which had been presented. The applicant alleged that what had been shipped was rubbish rather than any semblance of the goods contracted for.

Shientag J stated:

"However, I believe that a different situation is presented in the instant action. This is not a controversy between the buyer and seller concerning a mere breach of warranty regarding the quality of the merchandise; on the present motion, it must be assumed that the seller has intentionally failed to ship any goods ordered by the buyer. In such a situation, where the seller's fraud has been called to the bank's attention before the drafts and documents have been presented for payment, the principle of independence of the bank's obligation under the letter of credit should not be extended to protect the unscrupulous seller. It is true. that even though the documents are forged or fraudulent, if the issuing bank has already paid the draft before receiving notice of the seller's fraud, it will be protected if it exercised reasonable diligence before making such payment."

114. In similar circumstances, following the  Sztejn, Mr Berger J in Handerson vs Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Peat Marwick Ltd, 40 British Columbia LR 318 granted injunction to stop the bank from making payment under a letter of credit.

115. Facts of the case are that the plaintiff established an irrevocable letter of credit for purchase of 20 episodes of two television shows from a production company. Although the shows were never produced and the production company went into bankruptcy, the receiver of the seller made demand upon the bank for payment under the letter of credit and the plaintiff made an application for interlocutory injunction to stop the bank from making the payment. The Court granted injunction as prayed for. It held that the letter of credit is independent of the primary contract of sale between the buyer and seller. The issuing bank agreed to pay upon presentation of documents, not goods. There is one exception to this rule; that the bank should not pay under the credit where it knows that the request for payment is made fraudulently in circumstances when there is no right to payment. The case fell within this exception.

116. The decision in Sztejn was although delivered on July 1, 1941 but was cited as an authority on the principle of fraud exception before the English jurisdictions only in the last part of 1970s.

English cases:

117. Where the American Courts were more willing to adopt and apply the concept of fraud, the English Courts appears to go slow in recognising first and then applying the exception. In Hamzeh Malas & Sons vs British Imex Industries Ltd. [1958] 2 QB 127 Mr Sellers J while concurring the judgment refusing injunction observed that 'There may well be cases where the Court would exercise jurisdiction as in a case where there is fraudulent transaction'.

[1975] 1 All ER 1071 i.e. after 34 years of the application of the exception in American Court. In the case, the plaintiffs brought an action against the defendants, alleging that the French company had been guilty of fraud, and sought interlocutory injunction restraining them from paying the draft drawn on them by the French company or from paying out any sums to the French company or to any party pursuant to the irrevocable letter of credit.

In refusing injunction, Mr Megarry, J thought,

"I would be slow to interfere with banker's irrevocable credits, and not least in the sphere of international banking, unless a sufficiently grave cause is shown; for interventions by the court that are too ready or too frequent might gravely impair the reliance which, quite properly, is placed on such credits. The Sztejn case is plainly distinguishable in relation both to established fraud and to the absence there of any possible holder in due course. I do not say that the doctrine of that case is wrong or that it is incapable of extension to cases in which fraud is alleged but has not been established, provided a sufficient case is made out. That mayor may not be the case. What I do say is that the present case falls far short of establishing any ground on which it would be right for the court to intervene by granting the interlocutory injunction claimed, even in its revised form. The motion accordingly, failed and will be dismissed."

What weighed heavily with the Court in refusing injunction is that the payment would not harm the plaintiffs so long the money does not come out of the plaintiffs funds. And if the first defendant i.e. the bank, acted in breach of the contract, the plaintiffs would have their claim against them. Though the Court recognised the possibility of existence of the exception based on fraud but had a doubt on right of the applicant to seek for an injunction on such exception. But it thought the exception could be sought for as a defence against payment. Such limitation in thought in the application of the exception based on fraud did not find any support in subsequent cases.

132. The decision of the House of Lords in United City Merchants vs Royal Bank of Canada appears to have been relied upon by the Court of Appeal.

133. Question precisely Was whether the Court should boldly hold that equity should not allow Paribas or Santander to raise the fraud defence against an assignee for value without notice.

Lord Justice Waller reasoned

"In my view, the position is that Santander had no authority to negotiate from Pari bas to discount, and did not' seek it. It was something they were entitled to do on their own account. If they had not chosen to discount and had waited until 27th November, they would have had a defence, and it is in those circumstances not open tothem to claim reimbursement from Paribas.

If a confirming bank in the position of Santander wishes to be free to give value for documents when it accepts the documents, it can do so either by insisting on the use of an acceptance credit or by insisting on obtaining authority to negotiate and, confirmation of reimbursement if it does. ... if Santander had informed Pari bas that it had discounted, and had received confirmation from Pari bas that Paribas would still reimburse on 27th November 1998, Paribas would not be able to raise the fraud exception because they would be estopped from disputing Santander's authority to discount."

134. Close reading of the English cases makes it clear that the Courts there generally recognised the exception based on fraud to the independence and sanctity of the letter of credit only in respect of which the beneficiary had knowledge. But when fraud is committed by a third party of which the beneficiary was not aware was not recognised as a defence or claim to refuse payment by the paying bank.

135. The House of Lords also confirmed second exception on limited area of international comity based on the Bretton Woods Agreement. The House of Lords however, ignored the issue of material inaccuracy and thereby rejected the proposition that the bank need not to pay if the documents presented for payment contained any material statement that was inaccurate. The anxiety reflected behind the decisions is that the buyer as an innocent should be protected from such fraud and the loss should be borne by the seller or beneficiary. It also missed to decide the issue when documents presented for payment that are inaccurate in material particular should. they constitute a breach of the contract between the seller and the issuing and/or paying bank entitling the bank to refuse payment. It also stopped to distinguish between the holder in due course and the beneficiary. We hope the law will not stop there. It is a living science and will definitely go forward charting through the multifarious challenges to life that come on the way.

136. Indian Jurisdiction:

Fraud exception was also recognised in the Indian Jurisdiction since long. In UP Co-operative Federation Ltd vs Singh Consultants and Engineers (P) Ltd, [1989] 65 Company Cases 283. the Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal and reversed the High Court decision which interfered with the invoking of two performance guarantees on the failure of the respondent in completing the work as stipulated and restored the order of the trial Court dismissing a prayer for restraining the invoking of the guarantees and encashing the bank guarantees. Mr Sabyasachi, J writing the opinion for the Court was of the view.

"An irrevocable commitment either in the form of confirmed bank guarantee or irrevocable letter of credit cannot be interfered with except in case of fraud or in case of apprehension of irretrievable injustice has been made out."

137. In the case, there was no fraud involved and no question either of irretrievable injustice was involved. He further considered the question, thus,

"If an element of fraud exists, then Courts can step in to prevent one of the parties to the contract from deriving unjust enrichment by invoking the bank guarantee."

138. In Federal Bank vs VM Jog Engineering Ltd. and others, AIR 2000 SC 3166: (2000) 1 SCC 663 the appellant bank negotiated the documents and released the amount due in favour of the sellers only after due certification of the genuineness of the documents by the issuing bank. But the buyers upon filing a suit obtained a temporary injunction against the issuing bank from honouring the letter of credit. Result being, the negotiating bank was stopped getting reimbursement from the issuing bank. Revision of the negotiating bank against the order was discharged by the High Court. Leave was granted by the Supreme Court of India to the negotiating bank. The plaintiff alleged no fraud or forgery against the negotiating bank or even knowledge of the fraud or forgery, which it alleged against the sellers in respect of delivery challans. Mr M Jagannatha Rao, J for the Court held that:

" .....if the appellant Federal Bank was merely a collecting bank or agent which had approached the bank of Maharashtra (the issuing bank) and if the issuing bank was sought to be restrained by the buyer before payment was made by the issuing bank to the collecting bank, the collecting bank could not have compelled the issuing bank to release the money for collection if the buyer informed the issuing bank in his plaint that the documents to be presented to it by the collecting bank were forged and fraudulent. But where, on the other hand, the negotiating bank, i.e. the Federal bank (appellant), has paid on the basis of a clearance given by the issuing bank as to genuineness of documents. and seeks reimbursement, then the negotiating bank is in the position of a holder in due course and the suit of the buyer must fail if it sought to restrain the issuing bank from reimbursing the negotiating bank. These principles prima facie follow from Shientag, J's judgment which has been followed both in England and by this Court, in several cases."

139. In Indian jurisdictions, the Courts have accepted the exceptions that exceed ambits of the fraud exception. Such cases are based on concepts such as 'special equities' and 'irretrievable prejudice' .

140. In Svenska Handelsbanken vs Messrs Indian Charge Chrome and others. (1994) 1 SCC 502 allowing an appeal against an order of injunction granted by the High Court against encashment of bank guarantees, Sabyasachi Mukharji, J observed,

"In order to restrain the operation either of irrevocable letter of credit or of confirmed letter of credit or of bank guarantee, there should be a serious dispute and a good prima facie case of fraud and special equities in the form of preventing irretrievable injustice between the parties; otherwise, the very purpose of bank guarantees would be negatived and the fabric of trading operation would be jeopardised."

141. In National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd vs Flowmore Pvt Ltd. (1995) 4 SCC 515 the Indian Supreme Court followed the same principle refusing injunction against invoking of the bank guarantees. It cited with approval the principle of irretrievable injustice as enunciated in the US case of Itek Corpn vs First National Bank of Boston. 566 Fed Supp 1210. It also cited with approval the observation of the Court in UP Cooperative Federation Ltd vs Singh Consultants and Engineers (Pvt) Ltd, (1988) 1 SCC 174 that the Court should not lightly interfere with a performance bond or guarantee unless there is fraud of the beneficiary and not somebody else.

142. All the cases of Indian Jurisdiction so far came to our notice were concerning interlocutory order of injunction. In Indian Jurisdiction, the consistent view is that in usual commercial transaction the commitments of the banks must be honoured without any interference by the Court. In exceptional cases of fraud or irretrievable injustice or special equities only the Court can interfere.

143. The above views find substantial support in our jurisdiction as well. Like Indian decisions, ours also related to interlocutory injunction in commercial transaction. But there was little or no scope for thorough consideration of the concept of fraud exception in wider perspective. In present cases, the fraud exception was raised as an issue at the trial of the suits.

<u>144. In summarising, we are of the view that an irrevocable letter. of credit constitutes a definite undertaking of the issuing bank, which it must honour and pay according to the terms and conditions of the credit. It is not concerned in the least with any dispute between the seller and buyer for any breach of the contract underlying the letter of credit. It is however, obliged to refuse payment when there is a clear fraud of which it has notice or knowledge. The Court shall not interfere with such irrevocable/confirmed commitment of such bank except in case of clear or established fraud or in cases of irretrievable injustice or special equities.</u>

174. In the circumstances, the conduct of the KEB also becomes relevant. It was submitted on behalf of the buyer and issuing banks that the KEB acted as a collecting bank of the seller and would not be entitled to any payment as agent for the fraud committed by its principal, seller.

175. The collecting bank is a bank which is requested by the beneficiary to present the documents under the credit on the beneficiary's behalf. It may act as collecting bank for two reasons. First, the beneficiary may prefer to use its own bank to forward the documents where they have to be presented abroad rather than forwarding them itself. It may also want to have the documents checked by the bank for compliance with the credit. Secondly, the beneficiary may have been financed by the bank to obtain the goods which are the object of the transaction underlying the credit. The collecting bank acts as the agent of the beneficiary for the purposes of presentation and receiving payment.

176. On the other hand, the negotiating bank is a bank which acquires the documents in its own right to be presented by it as a principal under the letter of credit which is a negotiation credit. A bank which purchases the documents under a negotiation credit may be called a negotiating bank. The essential distinction from a collecting bank is that a negotiating bank holds the documents in its own right. whereas a collecting bank holds them as agent for the beneficiary.

177. Whereas an issuing bank can look only to the applicant for reimbursement and if the documents which it has accepted do not conform to the credit it is at risk. and a confirming bank can only look to the issuing bank and is similarly at risk, a negotiating bank stands on the other side of the fence, that is to say, it stands on the beneficiary's side. The negotiating bank's position is closely allied to that of the beneficiary and unlike an issuing and a confirming bank, will ordinarily have recourse against the beneficiary if the credit fails to provide payment. as is discussed in the next two paragraphs.

(Documentary Credits by Raymond Jack and others, 2nd Edition at paragraph Nos. 7.2, 7.5 and 7.9).

Clause (f) of article 16 of the UCP 400. on which Mr Rezzaque heavily relied. provides, inter alia, that when the remitting bank draws the attention of the issuing bank to any discrepancies in the documents or advises the issuing bank that it has negotiated under reserve, the issuing bank shall not be thereby relieved from any of its obligations under any provision of this article. Such reserve concerns only the relations between the remitting bank and the party towards whom the reserve was made.

181. Article 1 provides, inter alia, that the articles of UCP 400 are binding on all parties 'unless otherwise expressly agreed'.

<u>182. When an express term of a contract comes into conflict with a provision of incorporated standard terms such term should normally be given effect on the ground that this was the term to which the parties gave special attention and such term should override a term which was incorporated only by reference. In other words, when the .letter of credit expressly contains a term, the parties thereto are expected and intended to act upon such term as they agreed and such term must be held to override a term of UCP 400 which is incorporated only by reference. In cross-examination of PW 1, Abul Kalam in FA 303 of 2000 stated that clause J was incorporated in the letter of credit outside all common banking practice.</u>

183. Clause J of the letter of credit in FA 303 of 2001 that "Discrepant document must not be negotiated even under reserve or guarantee without prior approval of the issuing bank." therefore, must be binding upon all parties thereto in overriding clause (f) of article 16 of UCP 400.

184. Similarly, clause J of the letters of credit dated 12-5-93 and 22-5-93 in FA 352 of 2001 that "Please add your confirmation at the beneficiary's cost" and special instruction.

"Upon negotiation of documents with the terms of the credit in the reimbursement, you are authorised to debit our Head Office NC with your New York Office on maturity under advice to us. Your draft is to be accompanied by a certificate stating that the terms and conditions of the credit have been complied with."

would come in the way to the claim of the KEB for payment under UCP 400.

185. In Royal Bank of Scotland pic vs Casso di Risparmio delle Province Lombarde, [1992] 1 Bank LR 251 at 256 Mr Mustill LJ stated,

"Nevertheless, whilst not belittling the utility of the UCP, it must be recognised that their terms do not constitute a statutory code. As their title makes clear that they contain a formulation of customs and practices, which the parties to a letter of credit transaction can incorporate into their contracts by reference. This being so, it seems to me that the obvious place to start, when searching for a contractual term material to a particular obligation, is the express agreement between the parties. If it is found that the parties have explicitly agreed to such term, the search need go no further, since any contrary provision in UCP must yield to the parties' express intention. If, on the other hand, the agreement is silent in the material respect, then recourse must be had to UCP, and if a relevant term is found there, that term will govern the case."

186. In view of above legal position on express terms in the letters of credit and on the evidence on record, we have no hesitation to say that the KEB accepted and/or negotiated the discrepant documents in violation of said clause J of the letter of credit in earlier appeal and without having any confirmation or authority in the latter.

187. It is on record that the KEB was the bank of the seller. No bank of experience in respect of international trade could have negotiated such documents without approval of the issuing bank had it not acted as a collecting bank. Secondly, if the seller is not entitled to payment then the KEB cannot claim in law payment from the PBL and/or ABBL under the letters of credit. Thirdly, in the aforesaid circumstances, the claim of KEB as holder in due course must be dismissed.

188. Last but not the least, in view of article 15 of UCP both PBL and ABBL failed to examine the drafts with the shipping documents with due diligence and sent acceptance of the documents which did not appear on their face to be in accordance with the above terms and conditions of the letters of credit. In such circumstances, if they are made to pay they would not be able to be reimbursed by the applicants, Gemini and/or Southern as the case may be since they acted against the instructions.

189. Besides, it was the case of both Gemini and Southern that the beneficiary, seller has already become bankrupt. By letters and faxes, fourth defendant Yulim Shipping Co. Ltd in both cases, an agent of said seller, accordingly informed them. They have also adduced those communications in evidence. Contrary thereto the KEB could furnish nothing excepting a denial. In view of such evidence, the trial Court did not commit any error accepting the case of the plaintiffs.

<u>190. Once the beneficiary is found to be bankrupt, the law enunciated in Handerson vs Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Peat Marwick Ltd, 40 British Columbia Lloyd's Rep 318; Itek Corporation vs First National Bank of Boston, 566 Fed Supp 1210 and National Thermal Power Corporation. Ltd vs Flowmore Pvt Ltd. [1995] 4 SCC 515 comes into play and the KEB would have no right to payment since its principal forfeited its right to such payment. And such payment would result in irretrievable injustice.</u>

By another telex dated 1-2-2000 fifth defendant, National Bank Limited, informed the applicant that the plaintiff Garb accepted the documents and payment of US $ 21,701.94 would be made on 15-4-2000.

201. It was further stated that since the documents were in order, appellant Hanvit negotiated the documents with third defendant BL Trading and paid in total US $ 71,274.14, the suit could not be decreed.

202. Mr Abdur Rezzaque, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submitted that since the documents were in order the appellant, Hanvit Bank, negotiated the documents with BL Trading Limited, third defendant and paid US $ 49,572.20 on 9-12-99 and US $ 21,701.94 on 17-12-99 making a total 71,274.14. The appellant was entitled to payment under the letters of credit as per  terms of UCP 500.

203. Secondly, he submitted that the ex parte judgment decreeing the suit did not give any reason whatsoever and such judgment in view of Order XX rule 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure must be held to be unreasonable and cannot be sustained in law. In support he cited the decision in the case of Bangladesh vs Israil Ali. 1981 BLD (AD) 371.

204. The learned Joint District Judge disposed of the suit in few lines. He recorded that he considered the deposition of PW 1 Syed Masudur Rahman and examined the documents adduced and found the case proved. Accordingly, he decreed the suit declaring title of the plaintiff against the defendants with injunction. He however, did not spell out what he meant by title or the injunction.

<u>205. The case raised serious questions of law and facts. The learned Joint District Judge did neither raise any issue thereto nor find time to give decision on such question of law or facts. His judgment reflects no application of mind. Even in ex parte disposal, a Court is not absolved of statutory obligation of writing a lawful judgment as required under rule 4(2) of Order XX of the Code of Civil Procedure. Discharge of judicial function in such slipshod and perfunctory manner was time and again deprecated but with little result. We are therefore, left with no choice but to reject such decision outright.</u>

206. Before parting, we must record our deep appreciation for thy  eftective assistance of learned Senior members of the Bar.

207. In the result, FA 303 of 2000 and FA 352 of 2001 are dismissed with costs and impugned judgments and decrees are hereby affirmed.

208. Send down the records at once.
